Incident Overview: The Sisi Fire is located in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest within a remote, steep, and rugged mountainous landscape. The surrounding area consists of forested slopes, drainages, and variable terrain near the communities of Lucerne, Holden Village, and Stehekin. The fire is burning in a mosaic of timber, timber understory, brush, and partially cured grasses, with abundant snags and heavy dead and down fuels. Fire behavior remains active, including backing, flanking, uphill and up-drainage runs, group tree torching, and spotting. The greatest potential for growth remains along the southern and eastern portions of the fire where active heat, continuous fuels, and steep terrain align.The U.S. Forest Service initiated an aggressive initial attack on the Sisi Fire using a Type 1 helicopter and rappeler support following a mid-August lightning storm. Although aerial firefighters achieved early success, progress halted due to severe hazards, including tree torching and rolling debris on 50% slopes. These conditions forced crews to disengage for their own safety. Following four days of active suppression efforts, critical fire weather triggered significant growth on August 20. Little Giant Fire resources will continue to respond and strategize its containment.A full-suppression strategy is being utilized, with tactics focused on keeping the fire within the smallest practicable footprint while providing the highest probability of success and minimizing risk to firefighters and aviators. Values at risk include Lucerne, Holden Village, Stehekin, recreation resources, infrastructure, and other natural and cultural resources. The Pacific Crest Trail remains closed between the North Cascades National Park/Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary and High Bridge along the Agnes Creek portion of the trail.Updates on alerts on closures:Forest: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest | Alerts | Forest ServicePark: Fire Closures - North Cascades National Park (U.S. National Park Service)

Incident Overview: Public Information Map (Pdf)      |     Morning Update (pdf)      |     Yosemite NP Air Quality    |    AirNow Smoke Monitoring     |     Operations Video Update     | The Dome Fire was reported on the morning of September 15, 2026. It is in the backcountry and located approximately 1/4 mile north of Chilnualna Falls and is visible from the Wawona Road (Highway 41).   Progress on the Dome Fire continues, with no change to the perimeter in several days. Containment has increased to 86%. Fire activity remains minimal, and any visible smoke is coming from interior pockets of heat.Firefighters on the east side will continue patrolling and mopping up today. Crews, mule trains, and helicopters will continue the task of removing hose and equipment from remote wilderness areas. Suppression repair work is underway to restore ground disturbed during firefighting operations, protecting sensitive natural and cultural resources and reducing the potential for erosion. Along secondary handlines, crews will pull berms back to match the natural terrain and scatter vegetation to help disguise the lines and limit water erosion.California Interagency Incident Management Team 4 is scheduled to transfer command of the fire back to Yosemite National Park on Thursday, October 15. Weather: A warming and drying trend is expected as high pressure builds across the area, with mostly light winds. Highs Tuesday will likely be in the 40s. Temperatures are forecast to climb into the 50s and approach the 60s Wednesday and Thursday.Temporary Trail Closure: Yosemite National Park is open and operating normally, with the following exceptions. Alder Creek Trail is open north to the Deer Camp Trailhead. Chilnualna Falls Trail is open from the trailhead east to Chilnualna Fall and Crescent Lake. All trails within the active fire footprint are currently closed, including all south and eastbound trails accessed from Glacier Point Road. Buena Vista Trail also remains closed at this time. The closed area can be seen on the public information map. The closure now also includes impacts to the Mono Meadow and Buena Vista Trails. View the full Closure Order, and Closure Order MapSmoke Impacts / Air Quality: No fire growth and low activity has improved smoke impacts across Yosemite NP and surrounding communities. Yosemite Valley experienced GOOD with brief periods of MODERATE smoke impacts again yesterday. Expect smoke impacts in Yosemite Valley to remain GOOD with very brief MODERATE smoke today. Expect overall GOOD smoke impacts continuing across the remainder of this outlook area. MODERATE ozone levels may continue to blow into Yosemite from the San Joaquin Valley in the afternoons. GOOD smoke impacts are expected to continue through the week.View current Air Quality Monitoring at https://fire.airnow.gov/#7/38.532/-119.416 Getting Supplies by Mule:  Several pack mules from the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, as well as from the Stanislaus National Forest t are being used to support firefighters on the Dome Fire. These intelligent, strong animals provide invaluable support. Using pack mules allows helicopters to do other work, such as bucket drops; and mules can also be used in smoky conditions where a helicopter would not have good visibility to deliver supplies to a remote site.  Read More!  Mule Video in Video GalleryManaging Fire Impacts in Federal Wilderness.    While it is widely understood that motorized equipment such as off-highway vehicles, dozers, or other mechanized equipment are not allowed in wilderness, this requirement is also largely true when fighting fires in wilderness.  Chainsaws, small portable water pumps and similar equipment is often allowed to operate during active fires, but large, ground disturbing equipment is still prohibited.  Firefighters use other methods, called Minimal Impact Suppression Tactics (MIST) when fighting fires in Wilderness areas.  Read more .Equipment Recovery and Backhaul:  While firefighters make the final push towards containment of the fire, they must fulfill another extremely important task.  Firefighters must be on the lookout for equipment in the field that is no longer needed by the crews that fought before them and recover and return items as activities continue to wind down.  The list of equipment that must be retrieved includes; hose, pump kits; generators; chainsaw kits; collapsible water tanks; and smaller items such as hose fittings and nozzles.  To gather these items, firefighters will GPS the location of equipment and then crews are sent out to backhaul these items.  Equipment must then be cleaned, repaired, and organized to be ready for the next incident.Drones and Aviation Safety:  A reminder: wildfires and drones don't mix.  Unauthorized drones can force firefighting aircraft to stop flying, delaying suppression efforts and allowing fires to grow. If you fly, we can't. Help protect firefighters, communities, and our nation's landscapes by keeping your drone away from wildfires.   Aviation resources "Own" the airspace around wildfires; the Temporary Flight Restriction for the Dome Fire is available at https://tfr.faa.gov/tfr3/?page=detail_6_4364  Know before you fly: https://knowbeforeyoufly.org/compliance.../avoid-wildfires/   Flight  Restriction Information https://www.faa.gov/uas/getting_started/temporary_flight_restrictions https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DoG956VMCto  - Specific Message from FAA Regarding Drones and Wildfireshttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-4qTrh7ZSY0 – NIFC Wildfire Drone Safety Videohttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4v5f4tH_HF4 What is a TFR – from a private drone YouTube page – https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WMy7ZzkhUJU – Federal Charges Brought against drone operator in California Palisades FireManagement Objectives Prioritize firefighter's and the public's safety through risk analysis and hazard mitigation. Minimize burned acres utilizing direct extinguishment tactics. Utilize resources where they can be most successful and ensure tactics have a high probability of success. Protect and minimize impacts to local communities. wilderness values, and cultural/natural resources. Provide timely and accurate public information.Since 1916, the National Park Service has been entrusted with the care of our national parks. With the help of volunteers and partners, we safeguard these special places and share their stories with more than 318 million visitors every year. But our work doesn't stop there.We are proud that tribes, local governments, nonprofit organizations, businesses, and individual citizens ask for our help in revitalizing their communities, preserving local history, celebrating local heritage, and creating close-to-home opportunities for kids and families to get outside, be active, and have fun.

Incident Overview: 2026 Prescribed Fire Operations The Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, along with interagency partners and neighbors, plans to implement prescribed fire projects, as weather and fuels conditions allow. Public and firefighter safety is the top priority in all prescribed fire operations. Fire managers develop burn plans accounting for safety, specific fuel and weather prescriptions, and smoke management. Prior to implementation, local fire managers coordinate with local cooperators, counties, and partners.  All prescribed burns are closely evaluated and are only approved when favorable conditions are present.Benefits of prescribed fire as a forest management tool:Protects communities and infrastructure by reducing hazardous fuels and the risk of future high-intensity wildfires.Mitigates future wildfire risk and promote resilient fire-adapted landscapes.Reduces build-up of flammable vegetation, dead and down trees, and overgrowth.Improves and supports wildlife habitat for many species on the Forest.Limits the spread of invasive plant species and minimizes the spread of pest insects and disease, maintaining native ecosystems.Recycles nutrients back into the soil.Promotes the growth of trees, plants, wildflowers, and other flora and fauna.Continues the historic, natural fire regime of periodic disturbance by fire in forested ecosystems. Prescribed fires are planned for various units across the Forest; however, the window of opportunity for prescribed fire implementation is affected by several factors. Safety factors, weather conditions, air quality, personnel availability, and environmental regulations are continually monitored before implementation to determine feasibility of moving forward with the prescribed fire operations, during implementation, and after completion of the unit(s). All prescribed fires will be implemented in compliance with Oregon air quality standards and coordinated with appropriate county health departments to reduce the impacts of smoke to neighbors, cooperators, and surrounding communities. Smoke may settle in valley bottoms and drainages overnight, but it is expected to dissipate within a few days. Visit the Fire and Smoke Map by AirNow for the current smoke outlook. Daily planned ignitions can be found on line at the PNW Prescribed Fire Tracker. Types of Prescribed FirePile Burning: ignition of hand or machine piles of cut vegetation that have been allowed to dry out. Pile burning is commonly used to mitigate wildfire risk in areas where broadcast burning may not be feasible, such as adjacent to communities or private lands. Piles are made from the residual woody debris often left after a mechanical thinning treatment and can range in size from small hand stacked piles to large piles created with mechanical equipment. Piles are typically burned in fall, winter, or early spring after the piles have dried out and conditions allow, reducing the damage to the remaining trees and confining the majority of fire to the footprint of the pile.Under-burning: a type of prescribed fire treatment, that ignites vegetation under the forest canopy and focuses on the consumption of surface fuels.

Incident Overview: 2026 Prescribed Burn Operations The Lolo National Forest, along with their interagency partners and neighbors, plans to implement prescribed fire projects, as weather and fuels conditions allow. Public and firefighter safety is the top priority in all prescribed fire operations. Fire managers develop burn plans accounting for safety, specific fuel and weather prescriptions, and smoke management. Prior to implementation, local fire managers coordinate with local cooperators, counties, and partners.  All prescribed burns are closely evaluated and are only approved when favorable conditions are present.Benefits of prescribed fire as a forest management tool:Protects communities and infrastructure by reducing hazardous fuels and the risk of future high-intensity wildfires.Mitigates future wildfire risk and promote resilient fire-adapted landscapes.Reduces build-up of flammable vegetation, dead and down trees, and overgrowth.Improves and supports wildlife habitat for many species on the Forest.Limits the spread of invasive plant species and minimizes the spread of pest insects and disease, maintaining native ecosystems.Recycles nutrients back into the soil.Promotes the growth of trees, plants, wildflowers, and other flora and fauna.Continues the historic, natural fire regime of periodic disturbance by fire in forested ecosystems. Prescribed fires are planned for various units across the Forest; however, the window of opportunity for prescribed fire implementation is affected by several factors. Safety factors, weather conditions, air quality, personnel availability, and environmental regulations are continually monitored before implementation to determine feasibility of moving forward with the prescribed fire operations, during implementation, and after completion of the unit(s). Types of Prescribed FirePile Burning: ignition of hand or machine piles of cut vegetation that have been allowed to dry out. Pile burning is commonly used to mitigate wildfire risk in areas where broadcast burning may not be feasible, such as adjacent to communities or private lands. Piles are made from the residual woody debris often left after a mechanical thinning treatment and can range in size from small hand stacked piles to large piles created with mechanical equipment. Piles are typically burned in fall, winter, or early spring after the piles have dried out and conditions allow, reducing the damage to the remaining trees and confining the majority of fire to the footprint of the pile.Under-burning: a type of prescribed fire treatment, that ignites vegetation under the forest canopy and focuses on the consumption of surface fuels.

Incident Overview: The Swiss Roll Fire was started by lightning on the Pagosa Ranger District of the San Juan National Forest, approximately 20 miles northeast of Pagosa Springs, CO. It is east of U.S. Highway 160, south of East Fork Road (CR 667) near Quartz Meadow.It was first discovered on August 20th and firefighters have not engaged in direct suppression tactics due to its remote location in stands of dead, beetle-killed timber. Falling trees are the number one cause of wildland firefighter fatalities and fire managers must weigh the threat of firefighters' lives against the fire's threat to values at risk (lives, property, and infrastructure). The Pagosa Ranger District is committed to its indirect suppression strategy on this fire and is taking suppression actions at predetermined points where crews can safely engage, including in Quartz Meadow. Significant moisture has occurred over the Swiss Roll Fire, and this has moderated fire activity significantly, however, there are still multiple areas of smoldering heat from heavy dead and down. The fire was declared 100% contained on October 1, 2026.The closure order has been lifted for the Swiss Roll Fire area. No closures are in effect.

Incident Overview: Summit Point Prescribed Burn Update: 10/08/202614:30 All ignitions are complete. A total of 89 acres have burned. Fire crews are now in a holding pattern to allow remaining material to fully consume, and have transitioned to patrolling all fire lines. Crews will remain on-site through Monday to continue patrol and secure all lines. Precipitation is expected over the burn area this coming weekend.Summit Point Prescribed Burn Update: 10/08/202613:00: Fire crews have completed 50% of the 89-acre burn unit. Environmental conditions remain very favorable with desired fire effects outlined in the burn plan.Summit Point Prescribed Burn Update: 10/08/202611:00 Test fire has been initiated within the Summit Point Burn Unit.11:00Test fire has been deemed successful.11:00 Main ignitions will be initiated.Summit Point Prescribed Burn Update: 10/07/202624‑Hour Public Notification: Summit Point Prescribed BurnPlanned Ignition Date: October 8, 2026 Location: Approximately six miles southwest of Slick Rock, Colorado, and 2.5 miles east of the Utah border on BLM‑managed lands. OverviewThe U.S. Wildland Fire Service, in coordination with the Bureau of Land Management’s Tres Rios Field Office, plans to implement the Summit Point Prescribed Burn tomorrow, Thursday, October 8, 2026, pending favorable weather and fuel conditions. This burn is part of an ongoing effort to reduce hazardous fuels, improve wildlife habitat, and restore ecological health across public lands in southwest Colorado.Project Details• The Summit Point burn unit consists primarily of pinyon–juniper mastication units, including Unit 7 (126 acres) and Unit 6 (15 acres).• Prescribed fire operations will occur only when conditions meet all approved burn‑plan parameters related to weather, fuel moisture, smoke dispersion, and personnel availability.• Fire personnel will remain on scene throughout ignition operations and will patrol the burn area afterward to ensure public safety.What the Public Can Expect• Smoke may be visible in the surrounding area, especially during active burning and into the evening as temperatures cool, and smoke settles into low‑lying areas.• Travelers along nearby routes may see personnel, vehicles, and smoke; no closures are anticipated at this time.• Residents and visitors are encouraged to monitor air quality resources if sensitive to smoke.----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Summit Point Prescribed Burn Update: 9/25/2026The U.S. Wildland Fire Service will be conducting prescribed‑fire operations on BLM‑administered public lands northwest of Egnar, within the Summit Point project area. Treatment will focus on Unit 7 (126 acres) and Unit 6 (15 acres)—both pinyon‑juniper mastication units identified for fuels reduction and ecosystem restoration.Planned ActionsBroadcast‑burn operations will occur only when favorable weather, fuel moisture, and resource conditions align with the approved burn‑plan prescription. Fire crews will use controlled ignitions to consume residual slash and surface fuels within mastication units, improving woodland health and reducing potential for high‑intensity wildfire.Smoke‑management requirements and public‑notification guidance for the Summit Point project are detailed in the project’s smoke permit.Objectives• Reduce hazardous fuel loading across mechanically treated pinyon‑juniper stands• Improve ecological resilience and maintain treatment effectiveness after mastication work• Support long‑term fuels‑management objectives within the Tres Rios Field Office’s seasonal prescribed‑fire program• Enhance community protection and wildfire‑response conditions in the Summit Point–Egnar corridorSmoke InformationVisible smoke is expected during ignition operations and may settle into low‑lying areas during evening hours. Interior fuels within treated units may smolder for several days after ignition. All smoke‑management standards outlined by the Colorado Air Pollution Control Division will be followed.Current StatusNo ignition date has been set. Operations will begin once conditions fall within prescription and required notifications are completed. Additional public updates will be posted as burn windows develop.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------Update: 3/5/2026Seasonal weather patterns across the region are transitioning toward the cooler nights, steady daytime warming, and predictable humidity trends that support safe and effective prescribed burning. These improving conditions are creating operational windows suitable for conducting the Summit Point prescribed burn. The project includes six burn units totaling approximately 146 acres, which may be treated individually or in phases depending on daily weather and fuel conditions. As these favorable conditions develop, firefighters will take advantage of them to initiate broadcast burning within the established prescription parameters.Prescribed fire remains one of the most important tools for maintaining the health and resilience of fire‑adapted ecosystems. Good fire reduces hazardous fuel accumulations, improves forest structure, and helps restore ecological processes that have been limited due to decades of fire exclusion. By applying fire in a deliberate and controlled manner, land managers can reduce the risk of high‑severity wildfire and maintain a landscape that is more resilient and easier to manage under future fire conditions.Smoke from prescribed burns is typically short‑lived and significantly less impactful than the prolonged, heavy smoke produced during uncontrolled wildfires. Implementing prescribed fire now helps limit the potential for long-duration smoke events and reduces the need for costly wildfire suppression efforts. Overall, prescribed fire is a cost‑effective and proactive approach to protecting nearby communities, natural resources, and long-term ecosystem health.Stay tuned and informed for future notifications about upcoming burning planned for the Summit Point project.
